items.goal: Add a signed-in My account page at /user/account in the WebApp that shows the user's name, email and shipping address from their claims, and link to it from the user menu above My orders.
items.modelReason: Small but user-facing Blazor work that has to follow the existing page conventions.
items.verifyReason: New page and user-menu change; the verifier signs in as alice and bob and checks the rendered values and the sign-in redirect.

alternatives.reason: Not needed: every required value is already in the WebApp's sign-in claims, and checkout uses them the same way.

alternatives.option: Delegate to separate page and menu subtasks
alternatives.reason: Too small to split; the two pieces are tightly linked.

subject: pair-implementer
reason: The menu link, title, header, name, address, bob isolation and the sign-in redirect all work, but the Email field is empty for both alice and bob because the page reads the raw 'email' claim type, which the WebApp's inbound claim mapping most likely renames.

items.reason: The Email field renders empty for alice (should be 'AliceSmith@email.com') and for bob (ac4-bob-account.png). Identity issues JwtClaimTypes.Email ('email'), but the WebApp's OIDC handler keeps the default inbound claim type map (Extensions.cs:58 only removes 'sub'), so the claim most likely arrives as ClaimTypes.Email and ReadClaim("email") finds nothing.
items.fix: Read the email from ClaimTypes.Email with a fallback to 'email' (e.g. ReadClaim("email") ?? ReadClaim(ClaimTypes.Email)), then check in the browser that alice shows AliceSmith@email.com and bob shows BobSmith@email.com.

items.reason: .account has no max-width: var(--content-max) / margin: 0 auto like .orders, so on very wide viewports the content is not centred within the same width as other pages.
items.fix: Constrain the container the same way other pages do, via a shared rule in wwwroot/css/app.css rather than copying the Orders rule.

items.title: User menu lists "My account" directly above "My orders"
items.reason: AC1 fixes the link's position in the user menu; a link added in the wrong place or missing fails the story's entry point. The menu only exists in the rendered WebApp for a signed-in user, so e2e is the cheapest layer.

items.title: "My account" link opens /user/account
items.reason: AC1 requires the link to open `/user/account`; a wrong href would leave the page unreachable from the UI. Separate from TC-01 because it checks navigation, not menu layout.

items.title: Account page heading is "My account" and tab title is "My account | AdventureWorks"
items.reason: AC2 states the exact heading and browser tab title, matching the `<page> | AdventureWorks` convention of `/user/orders`. Only the rendered page shows the document title, so e2e.

items.title: Account page shows alice's name, email and shipping address
covers: AC2: address "15703 NE 61st Ct, Redmond, WA 98052, U.S."
items.reason: The core value of the story: the shopper sees the details orders are placed with. It checks the name join (first + last), the email claim and the exact address format ("street, city, state zip, country"), which is the same address checkout fills in. Values come from the identity claims of a real sign-in, so e2e.

items.title: Account page shows bob's own name and email and none of alice's
items.reason: AC3 guards against the page showing a fixed or another user's details; a hard-coded or cached value would leak alice's data to bob. Uses a fresh browser context so only bob's session exists.

items.title: After alice logs out and bob signs in in the same browser, the page shows only bob's details
covers: AC5: Log out works as today
items.reason: AC3 in the realistic shared-browser case: if the page or circuit kept the previous user's claims, alice's details would show to bob. Distinct from TC-05, which starts from a clean context.

items.title: Anonymous visitor opening /user/account is sent to sign in
covers: AC4: visitor not signed in is sent to sign in
items.reason: AC4: the page shows personal data and must require authentication; a missing `[Authorize]` would render the page (possibly empty) to anyone. The redirect is the OIDC challenge, observable only through the browser on the stack.

items.title: Signing in as alice from the redirect lands on /user/account
covers: AC4: after signing in as alice they land on /user/account
items.reason: AC4's second half: the return URL must be preserved through the OIDC round trip, otherwise the user lands on the home page. Separate from TC-07 because it checks the return, not the refusal.

items.title: "My orders" is still in the user menu and opens the orders page
covers: AC5: "My orders" still there and works
items.reason: AC5 is a regression guard: adding the new link must not break the existing "My orders" entry. Separate from the logout case so a failure names the broken item.

items.title: "Log out" is still in the user menu and signs the user out
covers: AC5: "Log out" still there and works
items.reason: AC5 regression guard for the logout form that sits next to the new link. Checking that `/user/account` then demands sign-in proves the session really ended.
